1.pericope_label: And it came to pass the same year, in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fourth year, and in the fifth month, that Hananiah the son of Azur the prophet, which was of Gibeon, spake unto me in the house of the Lord, in the presence of the priests and of all the people, saying, Thus speaketh the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, saying, I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon. Within two full years will I bring again into this place all the vessels of the Lord’s house, that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon took away from this place, and carried them to Babylon: And I will bring again to this place Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim king of Judah, with all the captives of Judah, that went into Babylon, saith the Lord: for I will break the yoke of the king of Babylon.

schools.summary: Ellicott confirms that the chapter follows immediately on the preceding one and that the royal name at its head is a copyist's slip, reports that nothing is known of Hananiah beyond this record, places him among the leaders of the party of resistance whose hopes had revived with the new Egyptian king, and draws three inferences from Gibeon: that it lay in the prophet's own tribe so the quarrel may be an old rivalry revived, that it was a priests' town so the man was probably a priest, and that it had once housed the tabernacle, a setting which should have taught him that no place is exempt; he also hears deliberate irony in the borrowed formula and reads the naming of the exiled king as a whole political programme.

Gill observes that the impostor described the Lord exactly as the true messengers do, a bold and daring act, and sees why restoring the exiled king would please a people who thought their present ruler a mere deputy; Calvin dwells on where the man stood, sanctuary around him and ark before him, asks whether he was a knowing fraud or a sincere bigot and answers that either way he served one master, describes the divine name tossed between two claimants as though the devil played with it, insists the two years means within and not at the end, and presses the awkwardness that a restoration required an abdication.

Clarke fixes the fifth month to the new moon of August, notes that the verse dates the preceding chapter and settles its corrupt royal name, calls the speech awful impudence in a man who knew he had no commission, and finds a grim irony in an interval that gave the enemy time to finish the city while the man who named it did not see it out; Wesley suspects a reckoning by the sabbatical cycle and infers the priesthood from the town.

Henry explains the apparent contradiction in the date by dividing the reign into a tributary beginning and a rebellious remainder, recalls the royal journey to Babylon that raised false hopes, notes that the challenger faced Jeremiah and addressed the speech to him, and weighs the sermon itself and finds the piety missing: prosperity promised with no word of repentance or prayer, temporal mercies detached from the spiritual ones that always accompany them.

debates.question: How can the fourth year be called the beginning of the reign?

positions.position: The first four years were the beginning because through them the king reigned as a tributary; the rebellion made the latter part.
The reckoning is probably by the sabbatical cycle.

outliers.claim: Draws a moral from Gibeon's history as the old home of the tabernacle: a man raised among those relics should have learned that no place, however sacred, is exempt from change.
Judges the false sermon by what it omits rather than what it claims, finding no counsel to repent, reform or pray, and no spiritual mercy joined to the temporal ones.

5.pericope_label: Then the prophet Jeremiah said unto the prophet Hananiah in the presence of the priests, and in the presence of all the people that stood in the house of the Lord, Even the prophet Jeremiah said, Amen: the Lord do so: the Lord perform thy words which thou hast prophesied, to bring again the vessels of the Lord’s house, and all that is carried away captive, from Babylon into this place. Nevertheless hear thou now this word that I speak in thine ears, and in the ears of all the people; The prophets that have been before me and before thee of old prophesied both against many countries, and against great kingdoms, of war, and of evil, and of pestilence. The prophet which prophesieth of peace, when the word of the prophet shall come to pass, then shall the prophet be known, that the Lord hath truly sent him.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch trace the reply as a piece of reasoning, the desirability of the prediction granted first and the record of every earlier prophet then put in evidence, so that a man predicting nothing but safety stands against the whole line of witnesses; Ellicott calls the argument frankly inductive, gives the burden of proof to those holding out flattering hopes, hears keen and incisive irony in the Amen, notes that the word for peace covers every kind of national wellbeing and so stands opposed to famine and plague as much as to war, and finds the language of the law behind the whole test.

Gill takes the Amen at face value, a countryman's wish qualified by a prophet's knowledge that it could not be, and what was really wanted was the repentance that would make threat and promise both unnecessary, adding that a preacher of prosperity is always agreeable to his hearers; Calvin explains why the reply was needed at all, since a people handled roughly wants flattery and resents being called to account, shows how the two attitudes coexist without hypocrisy in men given a heroic greatness of mind who did not put off human feeling with it, prefers famine to evil as the middle term of the three on manuscript evidence, and refuses to let the test of fulfilment stand alone.

Clarke reads the Amen as an open-hearted wish that the people might find it true, fills in the roll of the earlier prophets who denounced the same evils, and states the criterion sharply: a true prophet names the thing and fixes the term, and he sets two years for the return of vessels and captives against one year for the city's fall and seventy before any restoration.

debates.question: In what spirit was the Amen spoken?

positions.position: Sincerely, as a countryman's wish, though as a prophet he knew it could not be; what he really wanted was their repentance.
As an open-hearted wish that the people might find it true.
With keen and incisive irony: the wish could be echoed honestly as a wish, but he knew it impossible and thought it unwise to pray against a declared purpose.

debates.question: Does fulfilment by itself certify a prophet?

positions.position: Yes: he is a true prophet who names the thing and fixes the term, and both come out as named.
No: the same law warns that a prediction may come true and the man still not be believed, the event being a trial of faith, since impostors sometimes tell the truth.
The test of the law is in view, and the antecedent probability favours the prophet who speaks as the older prophets did.

outliers.claim: Prefers famine to evil as the middle term of the three judgments, noting that more than twenty manuscripts read it so although the versions run the other way.
Puts the burden of proof on the preacher of peace rather than on the preacher of calamity, because the honoured older prophets had not spoken smooth things.

10.pericope_label: Then Hananiah the prophet took the yoke from off the prophet Jeremiah’s neck, and brake it. And Hananiah spake in the presence of all the people, saying, Thus saith the Lord; Even so will I break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the neck of all nations within the space of two full years. And the prophet Jeremiah went his way. Then the word of the Lord came unto Jeremiah the prophet, after that Hananiah the prophet had broken the yoke from off the neck of the prophet Jeremiah, saying, Go and tell Hananiah, saying, Thus saith the Lord; Thou hast broken the yokes of wood; but thou shalt make for them yokes of iron.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch place the fresh commission not long after the departure and treat what follows as the Lord's formal testimony against the man; Ellicott reads the interval as silent suffering and prayer answered, states the principle that resistance to a power which was for the time the scourge and so the servant of God could only produce a heavier bondage, and hears in the iron yoke an echo of the law's curse.

Gill calls the seizing of the yoke impudent and insolent, the worse because the thing was made and worn at command, supposes the prophet had retired to his lodging and leaves the mode of the revelation open, and lists what had been abused: the name, the messenger, the message and its emblems; Calvin calls the act sacrilege against a visible attestation that worked like a sacrament, observes that once a man dares resist the word he spares none of the emblems of that power, presses the craft of a performance that imitated the true prophets by joining sign to teaching, makes the withdrawal deliberate policy since nothing can be heard in a tumult, and worries at the grammar of the reply.

Clarke puts the acted sign in one line, that it was meant to make the prediction credible, and reads the iron yoke practically as subjection tightened rather than lifted, with property taken and even the livestock handed over; Wesley reduces the whole exchange to a sentence, that the gesture incensed God further and made the judgment heavier.

Henry sees a calculated affront in the breaking, a sign produced to answer the sign already given so that the challenger appeared to win on his opponent's ground, finds the lying spirit borrowing the very formula of the Spirit of truth, leaves open whether the man believed his own message or merely worked on his hearers, and praises the patience of one who being reviled did not revile again.

debates.question: Why did the true prophet walk away without answering?

positions.position: Patience: being reviled he did not revile again, and would not wrangle with a man at the height of his fury before a hostile crowd.

Policy: prolonging the quarrel would have kindled contention on every side, nothing can be heard in a tumult, and returning under a fresh commission carried authority a shouting match would have cost.
An interval of silent suffering and prayer, to which the word of the Lord came as the answer.

outliers.claim: Contrasts the impostor with the ceremonies he saw in the church of Rome, which in his judgment please the eye and neglect the ear, whereas this man supplied sign and teaching together and so could deceive people who were not stupid.
Would read the abrupt sentence as the Greek version does, with the making of the iron yokes in the first person, a difference of one letter, and appeals to the requirement of the passage as a guide.

themes: Then Hananiah the prophet took the yoke from off the prophet Jeremiah’s neck, and brake it.

Then the word of the Lord came unto Jeremiah the prophet, after that Hananiah the prophet had broken the yoke from off the neck of the prophet Jeremiah, saying,

14.pericope_label: For thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel; I have put a yoke of iron upon the neck of all these nations, that they may serve Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon; and they shall serve him: and I have given him the beasts of the field also. Then said the prophet Jeremiah unto Hananiah the prophet, Hear now, Hananiah; The Lord hath not sent thee; but thou makest this people to trust in a lie. Therefore thus saith the Lord; Behold, I will cast thee from off the face of the earth: this year thou shalt die, because thou hast taught rebellion against the Lord. So Hananiah the prophet died the same year in the seventh month.

schools.summary: Ellicott points out that the verb of sentence is literally I send thee, the same word as in the accusation and repeated with pointed irony, allows that the term named leaves room for repentance while suspecting that shame at exposure helped bring the end on, classes the episode with the commission to root out and pull down, sets beside it the strokes that fell on Ananias and on Elymas, infers an interval of some days since the temple scene, and finds a strange significance in the same official title being given to true and false alike.

Gill guesses at a public meeting place, the point being the conviction of onlookers as much as the confusion of the man, and states the bare logic of the ending, that death in the year named proved one false and the other true; Calvin refuses to let the iron band stand as bare theatre, explains the change of material by the crowd's consent to the profanation of the wooden sign, draws the rule that those who bark at God only double their sentence, generalises the necessity of confrontation to his own day since simple minds fluctuate while two parties are in conflict, admires the brevity of a refutation that needed only the charge of not having been sent, gathers the versions of the closing charge, and is struck that a man was driven out of the world by the sound of a tongue with no hand laid on him.

Clarke measures the courage of the confrontation before priests and people already partial to a man who told them what they liked, remarking that in such cases men wish to be deceived, turns the sentence into a public test of not seventy years nor two but this year within two months, and reads the interval between the fifth month and the seventh as mercy, time to prepare to meet a judge, adding that the fulfilment must have won credit for everything else the true prophet had said; Wesley draws the lesson for ministers who teach against a revealed will.

debates.question: What was the interval between sentence and death for?

positions.position: Mercy: about two months in which the condemned man might prepare to meet his judge.
Room for repentance, though shame at exposure may itself have helped bring the stroke on.
A demonstration to the perplexed who could not judge between the claimants, and the removal of any plea of ignorance.

outliers.claim: Reports and dismisses the rabbinic suggestion that the disciples secretly removed the body so that the people never learned of the death, since the narrative treats the event as public knowledge.
Likens those who resist God to a snared dog that struggles until it strangles itself, so that the wooden yoke broken becomes an iron one.
